cases.text: How much juice is in a lime?
checks: Gives an approximate kitchen quantity with units; acknowledges size/juiciness variation
cases.raw_text:
About 2 tablespoons, or 1 ounce, of juice is typical for one medium lime.
===MORE===
A medium lime usually gives about 2 tablespoons of juice, which is about 1 fluid ounce or roughly 30 milliliters.

As a quick rule:
1 lime = about 2 tablespoons
2 limes = about 1/4 cup
4 limes = about 1/2 cup

Small or dry limes may give less, and very ripe juicy ones can give a bit more.
cases.spoken: About 2 tablespoons, or 1 ounce, of juice is typical for one medium lime.

cases.text: How should I serve an apple to a one-year-old, according to Solid Starts?
checks: Retrieves and attributes Solid Starts rather than inventing its recommendation
Age-appropriate preparation; does not recommend raw chunks or wedges for a one-year-old
Distinguishes the source's thin raw slices/grated options from soft cooked apple
cases.reference_notes: Checked 2026-09-12: source's 9+ month section permits cooked sections, grated raw apple, thin rounds or half-rounds, with or without skin. Whole apples discussed at 18+ months; wedges at 24+ months with readiness qualifications.
cases.raw_text:
For a one-year-old, Solid Starts says to offer apple as soft cooked pieces, or if it’s raw, grate it or cut it into very thin round or half-round slices. Not raw chunks, wedges, or a whole apple yet.

===MORE===
According to Solid Starts’ apple page, a 12-month-old fits their 9 months+ serving guidance for apple. At that stage, they say to continue offering sections of cooked apple, and for raw apple, to serve it grated or in thinly sliced rounds or half-round slices, with or without the skin. They suggest making the slices just thick enough that they don’t flop over when held. ([solidstarts.com](https://solidstarts.com/foods/apple/))

Solid Starts also warns that raw apple is one of the top choking hazards for children under 3. Their later stages are different: whole apples are suggested only from about 18 months+ if the child is clearly ready, and raw wedges or quartered sections are typically not until sometime after age 2. ([solidstarts.com](https://solidstarts.com/foods/apple/))
cases.spoken: For a one-year-old, Solid Starts says to offer apple as soft cooked pieces, or if it’s raw, grate it or cut it into very thin round or half-round slices. Not raw chunks, wedges, or a whole apple yet.

cases.text: What about with the skin on?
checks: Accurately represents the named source: skin is permitted for the thin raw slices in its 9+ month section
Does not turn skin permission into permission for thick raw pieces
cases.raw_text:
Yes — for a one-year-old, Solid Starts says raw apple can be served with the skin on, as long as it’s grated or cut into very thin round or half-round slices. If the skin seems hard for your child to manage, peel it. 

===MORE===
Solid Starts says that for babies 9 months and up, raw apple may be served “grated or in thinly sliced rounds or half-round slices, with or without the skin,” and a one-year-old falls in that range. They say to make the slices thick enough that they don’t flop over when held. ([solidstarts.com](https://solidstarts.com/foods/apple/))

They also note that many babies will chew on the skin and spit it out, and that the skin can help the apple hold together while baby munches. ([solidstarts.com](https://solidstarts.com/foods/apple/))

Solid Starts still warns that raw apple is a top choking hazard for children under 3, so avoid raw chunks, wedges, or a whole apple at this age. ([solidstarts.com](https://solidstarts.com/foods/apple/))
cases.spoken: Yes — for a one-year-old, Solid Starts says raw apple can be served with the skin on, as long as it’s grated or cut into very thin round or half-round slices. If the skin seems hard for your child to manage, peel it.

cases.text: Can I substitute baking soda for baking powder in pancakes?
checks: Explains not a direct one-for-one substitution
Baking soda needs acid; baking powder contains an acid component
Avoids prescribing an unconditional replacement ratio without recipe context
cases.raw_text:
Yes, but not one-for-one. Baking soda needs an acid to work, so only use it if your pancake batter has something acidic like buttermilk, yogurt, or lemon juice.

===MORE===
You can substitute baking soda for baking powder in pancakes, but they are not equivalent ingredients.

Use this rule:
- 1 teaspoon baking powder = about 1/4 teaspoon baking soda, plus enough acid in the batter

Why:
- Baking powder already contains both a base and an acid
- Baking soda is only the base, so it needs an acidic ingredient to create lift

Good acidic ingredients for pancakes:
- Buttermilk
- Yogurt
- Sour cream
- Lemon juice
- Vinegar, in a small amount

If your recipe uses regular milk and has no acid, baking soda alone is not a good substitute. The pancakes may taste soapy or not rise well.

Simple example:
- If a recipe calls for 1 teaspoon baking powder, you can try 1/4 teaspoon baking soda plus buttermilk instead of regular milk.
cases.spoken: Yes, but not one-for-one. Baking soda needs an acid to work, so only use it if your pancake batter has something acidic like buttermilk, yogurt, or lemon juice.

cases.text: When I mix blue and red light from an LED strip, I see purple. Are the waveforms collapsing to an average wavelength, the same as a single purple wavelength, or are my eyes seeing purple while red and blue are still emitted separately?
checks: Red and blue spectral components remain; ordinary LED mixing does not average them into a new wavelength
Explains additive color perception through cone responses and brain interpretation
Distinguishes nonspectral purple/magenta from spectral violet
Does not confuse superposition with nonlinear frequency conversion or quantum collapse
cases.raw_text:
Your eyes are seeing purple while the red and blue light are still being emitted separately. They do not collapse into one “average” wavelength; your visual system combines those separate wavelengths into a color sensation.

===MORE===
What’s happening is additive color mixing.

A red LED emits light in one band of wavelengths, and a blue LED emits light in another band. In the air, those light waves just overlap; they do not merge into a new single wavelength. So physically, the light is still a mix of red photons and blue photons.

Your eyes have cone cells that respond to ranges of wavelengths, not to a single exact wavelength label. When red and blue light hit your retina together, they stimulate the cones in a pattern your brain interprets as purple or magenta.

A few key points:
- There is no single “average wavelength” being created.
- The spectrum from the LEDs is still two separate peaks: one red, one blue.
- A single-wavelength color has to lie somewhere on the visible spectrum, but “purple” or “magenta” is not a single spectral wavelength at all.
- Violet is different: violet can be a single short wavelength. Purple/magenta is usually a mixed-color perception.

So the short answer is: the LEDs keep emitting red and blue separately, and your brain perceives the combination as purple.
cases.spoken: Your eyes are seeing purple while the red and blue light are still being emitted separately. They do not collapse into one “average” wavelength; your visual system combines those separate wavelengths into a color sensation.
